Row.Text: Goryeo was the predominant Korean state from the 10th century CE until the end of the 14th and gives us the name “Korea” today. It incorporated Buddhism and Confucianism into broader Korean society, advanced Korean arts and sciences, and stood at a crucial crossroads in the power struggles that shaped East Asia.

In the first millennium CE, the “three kingdoms” of Silla, Baekje, and Goguryeo were shakily unified under Silla, a regime that divided its people up into rigid systems of categorization – by region, but also by its “bone-rank” system of nobility. As Silla devolved into inter-noble fighting, a young prince of the kingdom, to be known later as Kung Ye, was born marked by a prophecy that he would spell disaster. Kung Ye, having grown up sentenced to death but kept alive in hiding, launched a campaign against unstable Silla and declared Goguryeo’s independence.

But Kung Ye may have been mad. He proclaimed himself a new Buddha and hunted those who disagreed. Chaos bred insurrection, and Kung Ye fell to his own prime minister, Wang Kon. Wang Kon assumed the royal title Taejo and named his kingdom Goryeo.

Silla and Baekje were still major powers to Goryeo’s south, however, and Taejo’s first campaign was to make peace. He did this militarily, of course, but was careful to treat his defeated foes with magnanimity, incorporating the nobles of Baekje and Silla into the Goryeo system. In addition, he married the daughters of powerful regional lords, thus bringing them into the fold of Goryeo kinship as well as politics.

Goryeo society moved away from Silla’s customs towards a bureaucratic system, incorporating Confucian notions of civil service exams and education as a way to integrate regional nobility into a centralized state. Its society was stratified, with scholar-bureaucrats occupying significant positions, institutionalized slavery, and a tradition of civilian rule. Despite the Confucian influence, Buddhism remained vital to Goryeo life, and core Buddhist texts such as the Tripitaka were collected and published. Indeed, publishing was a strong suit of Goryeo, as Korean inventors adopted a system of metal moveable type (using Chinese characters – Korean script would have to wait until the Joseon dynasty for its birth). The most famous Goryeo art is its ceramics. Korean celadon was delicate and beautiful, often a jade-like green, and took the shape of light and organic forms.

In broader East Asia, Goryeo became a kingmaker. After defeating the Khitan-led Liao dynasty of China, Goryeo found itself a coveted ally in the Song-Liao competition over the Chinese Mandate of Heaven. It also became a global center for culture and commerce and brought in a significant Muslim population. But by the 12th century, cracks began to form. The aristocracy entered a period of infighting and military generals were able to seize significant amounts of power for themselves, staging a coup against the nobility and civilian rule in 1170. What followed was a military state – a step away from the rule of philosopher-kings and towards the rule of force.

Foreign developments were to bring an end to the military regime, but also an end to Goryeo’s independence. Following a Khitan invasion, the ascendant Mongol Empire (and the Mongol-led Yuan Dynasty of China) sought to increase control over the kingdom. When Goryeo objected, the Mongols invaded and a bloody, inconclusive war led to a tense peace. The military regime, though having successfully defended its borders, was weakened, and royalists managed to broker vassalage in 1270, signaling an end to military rule, but also to Goryeo’s independence.

With its fate thus tied to the Yuan Dynasty, Goryeo was caught up in its fall. As the Yuan Dynasty began to fracture, and the first glimmerings of what would be Ming appeared, the Goryeo King Gongmin decided to seize the opportunity to end Yuan domination in Korea. He purged Mongol influences at court and waged a war of expansion into Yuan territory. But this war was to end not at Chinese hands, but at those of one of his commanders, General Yi Song-gye. The general, soon to be King Taejo of Joseon, brought the Goryeo age to a close and began Korea’s long-lasting Joseon period.

The story of Buseok Temple – Buseoksa – begins not in Goryeo, but in Silla, with a monk named Uisang. Travels of monks from the rest of East Asia to China (and, occasionally, from China to India) were opportunities to introduce new schools of thought into Buddhism, and Uisang was no different. In the middle of the seventh century CE, Uisang studied the Hwaeom (Chinese: Huayan) tradition in China, a precursor to Seon (also known as Zen) and a branch of Mahayana thought, and began the journey back to Silla to share his learnings with other monks. On the way, though, dangers beset him, and it was through the intervention of a friendly dragon that he made his journey successfully. The dragon placed a floating rock – the buseok – at the gate to the temple, from which Buseoksa gains its name. Hwaeom became the principal school of thought in Goryeo, and a key legitimator of royal rule. The temple itself epitomized Hwaeom architecture, seeking to harmoniously blend itself into the landscape, rather than altering it by brute force. It remains to this day, in Yeongju.

Of all the arts of Goryeo, pottery has been the most renowned. Chinese celadon during the Song Dynasty, with its green-blue glaze so reminiscent of jade, became popular throughout the Sinitic world, with imitators across Korea, Japan, and other places touched by Chinese trade. But the kilns – the gama – in Goryeo brought local celadon production together with Chinese styles to create an artform that was truly unique. Goryeo kilns produced translucent, almost organic-seeming pieces. Korean craftsmen experimented with different kinds of clay, techniques such as stripping away a layer of glaze to reveal a pattern underneath, and shapes that evoked plants, dragons, lions, and turtles. Goryeo celadon has made it not only to international fame, but as National Treasures of Korea.

Wang Kŏn, the founder of Goryeo, rose to power in a coup d’etat – hardly the foundation of a stable political structure. With this in mind, he founded Goryeo on the principle of Cheonsu, a concept similar to the Chinese “Mandate of Heaven.” The claim of Cheonsu meant that the universe itself had sanctioned the Goryeo state, and that Wang Kŏn’s coup was not an act of individual ambition, but destiny. And perhaps he had a point: Wang Kŏn became king of the new state of Goryeo, founding a dynasty that would last, more or less, until the rise of the Yi dynasty and the Joseon era nearly five centuries later.

The Tripitaka is the Sanskrit name given to the Buddhist canon. The word means “triple basket,” referring to the three kinds of knowledge contained in them: sutras (sayings), rules for monastic conduct, and scholarly analyses. In particular, the Tripitaka Koreana is the term given to a greatly expanded Tripitaka printed via wood blocks in the 1000s. Each of the over 80,000 pages of the massive text was carved, making the project a colossal undertaking. But this was an undertaking done twice: the original blocks were destroyed during the Mongol invasion and redone in the 1200s.

78 years before the Gutenberg Bible was printed on moveable metal type, the Jikji was printed in Goryeo, making it the oldest such printed book in existence. Written by the monk Baegun, Jikji is an account of Buddhist thinkers meant for the instruction of Buddhist students – important, as Buddhism was vital to the Goryeo state. But here, the book itself is not the key factor, as the printing press allowed for the expansion and standardization of material to be distributed across the kingdom, although it would be only in Joseon that printing would be a central tool of statecraft.

Gunpowder was in use in East Asia for much of the medieval period, but it was the Mongols (and the Yuan Dynasty of China) that really spread early firearms in warfare, with incendiary arrows and gunpowder-propelled projectiles. In late Goryeo, engineers developed their own innovation, as deadly as it was simple: a handcart with a series of tubes, and each tube loaded with a fire arrow (or, in other variants, gunpowder-charged projectiles). Imagine a hundred arrowhead-tipped bottle rockets lined up on a handcart, awaiting a flame to send them towards the enemy, and you have imagined a hwacha. The weapon was used to repel Japanese pirates at the end of Goryeo, and again during the invasions of the Imjin wars in Joseon.

In the later part of the Goryeo period (after 1170 CE), the military assumed near-direct control, keeping a king as a figurehead over what was in practice a military state. This was in some part a reaction against the accumulation of perceived slights towards military figures in Goryeo society, as well as the perceived threat from the Mongols and Mongol-dominated Yuan China so near to the Korean border. This regime held its power via the tobang – military personnel tasked with policing civil officials and ensuring loyalty to the military (and its ruling Choe family). This militarized society successfully defended Korea against invasions by the Khitans and Yuan alike. The era of the tobang fell as royal elites brokered a diplomatic solution, ending the threat of a Chinese invasion and resulting in the subjugation of Goryeo as a vassal state to the Yuan.
